semantic_correction.stem: A client on long-term hemodialysis says, 'Dialysis controls my life. I have stopped seeing friends, and I do not enjoy things I used to.' Which nursing response is best?

options.A: Assess mood, coping, social support, and safety; acknowledge the dialysis burden; and connect the client with dialysis social-work, mental-health, or peer support as indicated.
options.B: Normalize the loss of interest and social withdrawal as expected consequences of dialysis, then focus on treatment attendance and laboratory results unless symptoms worsen.
options.C: Emphasize adherence to the dialysis schedule and diet first, and defer emotional assessment until the client has adjusted to the treatment routine for several more months.
options.D: Advise the client to manage emotional concerns outside the dialysis setting because kidney-care visits should focus on physical treatment rather than mood or social support.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. National Kidney Foundation guidance updated August 13, 2025 states that depression can occur in people receiving dialysis and may include persistent sadness, loss of interest, low motivation, social isolation, and difficulty following the treatment plan. NKF notes that social isolation and loss of independence can contribute to depression and that untreated depression can impair relationships, quality of life, attendance, dietary adherence, and other aspects of dialysis care. NKF specifically states that many dialysis centers have social workers who can offer support, help identify depression, and connect clients with therapists, peer programs, support groups, and other services. A May 5, 2026 NKF mental-health resource further emphasizes that kidney disease affects emotions, relationships, and well-being and that mental-health concerns are often overlooked in kidney care. Therefore the client's anhedonia and withdrawal warrant assessment of mood, coping, social support, and safety, with appropriate support/referral rather than normalization or delay. B is incorrect because these symptoms may signal depression and should not be dismissed as expected dialysis effects. C is incorrect because emotional assessment should not be postponed while clinically relevant symptoms are already present. D is incorrect because mental-health and social support are part of comprehensive dialysis care rather than issues to exclude from the kidney-care team.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Recognize loss of interest, social withdrawal, and distress about dialysis dependence as cues for psychosocial and depression assessment and connect the client with appropriate dialysis social-work, mental-health, and peer-support resources without dismissing symptoms as inevitable treatment effects.
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Depression and Dialysis: Symptoms, Treatment, and Support; Your Mind Matters: Mental Health and Kidney Disease; NKF Peers
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Depression and Dialysis last updated August 13, 2025; Your Mind Matters published May 5, 2026; current NKF resources verified August 22, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Depression and Dialysis → depression may cause sadness, loss of interest, hopelessness, low motivation, social isolation, and problems following treatment; contributors include social isolation and loss of independence; talking about feelings is part of dialysis care; dialysis-unit social workers can identify depression and connect clients to counseling, peer support, and services. Your Mind Matters → CKD affects emotions, relationships, and overall well-being; mental and behavioral health concerns may be overlooked; persistent sadness, anxiety, hopelessness, or detachment warrant reaching out to the health-care team. NKF Peers → peer support is available for people having a hard time on dialysis and for care partners.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Current NKF guidance directly supports psychosocial and depression assessment for dialysis clients with persistent loss of interest, social withdrawal, or distress and identifies dialysis social workers, mental-health professionals, support groups, and peer programs as appropriate resources.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the absolute-word and correct-answer length cues, rebuilt all four responses to closely matched length and specificity, freshly verified 2025-2026 NKF mental-health resources, and made timely assessment plus individualized dialysis psychosocial support the single best response.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests recognition and support of possible depression during long-term dialysis with one clearly best response, balanced alternatives, current kidney-care guidance, and no absolute-word or answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It recognizes clinically relevant depressive and isolation cues, assesses safety and coping, and uses the social-work, mental-health, and peer resources supported by NKF guidance.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Loss of interest and social withdrawal can be signs of depression and should not be normalized or assessed only if they later worsen.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. The client already has meaningful psychosocial symptoms; delaying assessment for months risks missing a treatable mental-health concern that can affect dialysis care.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. NKF specifically treats mental health, social work, and peer support as part of comprehensive dialysis care.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A uniquely combines timely psychosocial assessment, safety review, acknowledgment, and resource linkage; B normalizes symptoms, C delays assessment, and D incorrectly excludes mental health from dialysis care.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel nursing responses of comparable length and clinical specificity; the prior 'only'/'entirely' distractors and uniquely-long correct response were removed.
